seoTitle: How to View Udemy Video Transcript on Desktop
metaDescription: Study more efficiently on Udemy by using video transcripts. Learn where the Transcript button lives, how synced text and autoscroll work, and how to search within it.
intro: Reading along with a transcript instead of pausing a video repeatedly can make studying a Udemy course much more efficient, especially for dense or technical material. The feature is easy to miss because it sits as a small icon in the video player toolbar rather than a labeled button, and once it's open, the way the text syncs and highlights as the video plays isn't obvious until you've seen it. This guide walks through opening a course, finding the Transcript control, and using the synced, highlighted text to follow along or review a lesson without constantly hitting pause.

steps.heading: Open a course you're enrolled in
steps.body: From your Udemy dashboard, the "Let's start learning" section shows your most recent lecture with a play button and running time, making it the fastest way back into a course you've already started. Click into the lecture to open the video player, which is where every transcript control lives — there's no separate transcript page outside the player itself.

image.caption: The Udemy dashboard's "Let's start learning" panel, with your most recent lecture ready to resume.

steps.heading: Find the Transcript icon in the player toolbar
steps.body: Inside the video player, look at the row of small icons along the bottom-right edge, next to playback speed and settings. One of them is a document-shaped icon — hovering over it pops up a "Transcript" label confirming what it does, since there's no permanent text next to the icon itself. Clicking it opens the transcript panel on the right side of the player, replacing whatever was showing there before, such as the course content list.

image.caption: The video player toolbar, with a tooltip labeled "Transcript" appearing over the document icon next to playback settings.

steps.heading: Read along with the synced, highlighted text
steps.body: Once open, the transcript panel shows the lecture's full spoken content broken into short lines, with the line matching the current point in the video underlined and highlighted as it plays. This makes it easy to follow dense, fast-paced instruction — like a spreadsheet formula walkthrough — without rewinding every few seconds to catch a detail you missed the first time. An "Autoscroll" checkbox sits at the bottom of the panel and is checked by default, keeping the highlighted line in view as the video progresses.

image.caption: The transcript panel open beside the video, with the currently spoken line highlighted and an Autoscroll checkbox below.

steps.heading: Turn off autoscroll when you want to browse freely
steps.body: If you'd rather scroll back through earlier parts of the transcript without the panel jumping back to the current playback position, uncheck Autoscroll. This is useful when you're trying to relocate a specific instruction from earlier in the video — you can scroll at your own pace and click any line in the transcript to jump the video straight to that point, rather than dragging the seek bar and guessing.

steps.heading: Search for specific text within the transcript
steps.body: The transcript panel also includes a text-search option, letting you type a word or phrase and jump directly to where it's spoken in the video rather than scanning manually. This is the fastest way to relocate a specific term or step in a long lecture — searching "formatting" in a spreadsheet course, for instance, jumps you past unrelated sections straight to the part that covers it.

steps.heading: Pair transcripts with your own notes
steps.body: Because the transcript is just text, it's easy to copy a passage into your own notes or a separate summarization tool rather than retyping what the instructor said. Combining transcript access with note-taking or AI-assisted summarization can meaningfully cut down the time it takes to review a course before an exam or before applying what you learned at work.

steps.heading: Know when this feature matters most
steps.body: Transcripts are most valuable for technical or jargon-heavy lessons where a single mispronounced or misheard term can throw off your understanding, and for anyone studying in a noisy environment or a non-native language where reading alongside listening improves comprehension. For simpler conceptual lectures, you may not need the panel open at all — it's a tool to reach for when the material gets dense, not something to run permanently.

faq.question: Can I search for specific words in a Udemy transcript?
faq.answer: Yes, the transcript panel includes a search function that lets you jump directly to the point in the video where a specific word or phrase is spoken.

faq.question: Where is the Transcript button in the Udemy player?
faq.answer: It's a small document-shaped icon in the video player's bottom-right toolbar, next to playback speed and settings. Hovering over it shows a "Transcript" tooltip.

faq.question: Why would I use a transcript instead of just watching the video?
faq.answer: Transcripts let you revisit specific parts of a course or study efficiently without pausing the video repeatedly, which is especially useful for dense or technical material.

faq.question: What does the Autoscroll option do?
faq.answer: When checked, the transcript panel automatically scrolls to keep the currently spoken line in view. Uncheck it if you want to browse the transcript independently of playback.

faq.question: Can AI tools improve how I use Udemy transcripts?
faq.answer: Yes, combining transcripts with automated summarization or note-taking tools can help you retain and apply information more effectively after the course.
